newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hunts rebels holding 29 oil workers.
newsitem.headline: Peru hunts rebels holding 29 oil workers.

text.p: The Peruvian army on Sunday scoured a remote jungle in search of 29 oil workers believed kidnapped by Maoist Shining Path guerrillas, police and military sources said.

Foot patrols set out Sunday morning, while at least two helicopters joined the hunt in the dense and hilly River Ene zone of Peru's central jungle where the rebel column is thought to be hiding its hostages.
"It's a difficult zone," a military source in the region told Reuters by telephone. "The terrorists have hideouts under the ground, with traps nearby to know when we get close."

The military and other police sources said they had received reports from natives in the region that a heavily- armed Shining Path column of between 50 or 60 men captured the workers several days ago, probably Friday. The workers were apparently employed by local exploration company CGG under contract for French oil giant Elf.

"According to the report, the terrorists threatened them. Some of the workers didn't want to go with them, so they beat them," a national police source in the regional capital of Huancayo told Reuters in a telephone interview.

A journalist in the zone, who asked not to be named, told Reuters he had confirmed the kidnapping with natives living nearby who witnessed it, and with local authorities. "It seems Shining Path has taken the workers to a secret prison in the jungle," he added.
An anti-terrorist police source, also in Huancayo, confirmed reports had arrived that 29 or 30 workers had been reported kidnapped, and that army helicopters were searching for them.

"The information we have is that it is Sendero -- the attackers were shouting 'Long Live Sendero' -- although the zone is normally used by the MRTA," he said in a phone interview, referring to Peru's smaller guerrilla movement, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement.

The police and military officials said the hostages may include foreigners, but could not confirm this. Elf officials in Peru and France could not be reached for comment, while diplomatic sources in Lima said they had no information.
There was no official confirmation of the kidnapping from the Peruvian government.

Shining Path and the MRTA have been highly active in the dense and isolated jungle area, mainly populated by Ashaninka Indians, throughout a 17-year war on the state. Anti-terrorist police sources have said remnants of both groups -- severely reduced in recent years as a result of a government offensive -- were hiding in the zone.

The MRTA won world notoriety in December 1996 with the kidnapping of hundreds of guests at a Japanese embassy party. They held 72 hostages for 126 days until Peru's military stormed the ambassador's residence, killing the 14 rebels and freeing alive all but one of the captives.

Overshadowed by the MRTA during hostage crisis, Shining Path had been concentrating on regrouping forces and peasant education work, according to police. It was unclear what motives the kidnapping had.

The MRTA's international spokesman, Isaac Velazco, confirmed the kidnapping was not by his group. "In this case, it is not an action by the MRTA, or I would have heard about it," Velazco told Reuters by telephone from Germany. "I know that Shining Path is in the zone. but what could their political motives be? If they are economic motives, they've never done this before."
While the MRTA has been characterized by lucrative kidnappings, the Shining Path has generally raised money from involvement with drug-traffickers.
